'''''Liatris spicata''''', the '''dense blazing star''', '''prairie feather''', '''gayfeather'''<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.gardenia.net/plant/liatris-spicata-gayfeather | title = Liatris spicata | publisher = Gardenia.net | access-date = 24 July 2023}}</ref> or '''button snakewort''',<ref name = GRIN>{{GRIN}}</ref> is a herbaceous perennial [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Asteraceae]]. It is native to eastern North America<ref name="PLANTS">{{PLANTS |symbol=LISP |taxon=Liatris spicata}}</ref> where it grows in moist [[prairie]]s and [[meadow]]s.

The plants have tall spikes of purple flowers resembling bottle brushes or feathers that grow {{convert|1-5|ft|m|abbr=on}} tall. The species grows in [[hardiness zone]]s 3–8,<ref name="Plant Finder">{{Cite web |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=d780 |title=Liatris spicata  |website=Plant Finder |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |access-date=2016-10-28}}</ref> stretching from the Midwest to the East Coast, eastern and western Canada.<ref name="PLANTS" />

Common varieties include 'Alba' and 'Floristan White' which are white-flowering [[cultivar]]s<ref>{{cite web |first=Leonard |last=Perry |title=Liatris |url=http://pss.uvm.edu/pss123/perliat.html |publisher=University of Vermont}}</ref> on {{convert|18|in|cm|abbr=on}} tall spikes, 'Callilepsis' with long stems good for [[cut flowers]], 'Floristan Violett' with a strong stem and thick, violet flower spikes preferred by florists, and 'Kobold' which stays small in size with deep purple flowers.<ref name="Wisconsin Horticulture">{{Cite web |url=http://hort.uwex.edu/articles/liatris/ |title=Wisconsin Horticulture |last=Mahr |first=Susan |date=2010 |website=Wisconsin Horticulture |publisher=University of Wisconsin-Extension |access-date=2018-08-13}}</ref>

''Liatris spicata'' var. ''resinosa'' is found in the southern part of the species's natural range.<ref>{{eFloras|1|250068573|Liatris spicata |tribe=Eupatorieae |first=Guy L. |last=Nesom}}</ref> The variable plants have only 5 or 6 flowers per head and the heads are more widely spaced on the stems; these differences are more pronounced when the plants are found in drier and coastal habitats.<ref name="Gleason1963">{{cite book |author=Henry A. Gleason|title=The New Britton and Brown Illustrated Flora of the Northeastern United States and Adjacent Canada: Illustrated by Original Drawings |volume=3 |page=498 |date=1963 |publisher=New York Botanical Garden}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Liatris spicata'' is a garden flower in many countries around the world, grown for its showy purple flowers (pink or white in some cultivars). They bloom in July through August or September, depending on where in their range they are located.<ref name="Wisconsin Horticulture" /><ref name="NPIN">{{NPIN|LISP |access-date=2016-12-14}}</ref>

Under cultivation it is found under many names including button snakewort, Kansas gay feather, blazing star, Liatris callilepis.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.shootgardening.co.uk/plant/liatris-spicata|title = Liatris spicata Button snakewort Kansas gay feather Blazing star callilepis calilepis Gayfeather Care Plant Varieties & Pruning Advice}}</ref>

Full sun is best and well-drained soil is preferred to prevent rot, though the plants do prefer moist soil. However, the plants do not tolerate wet soil in winter.<ref name="Hadley & Levin-1967">{{Cite journal|last=Elmer B. Hadley and Donald A. Levin|date=May–June 1967|title=Habitat Differences of Three Liatris Species and Their Hybrid Derivatives in an Interbreeding Population|jstor=2440658|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume= 54| issue = 5|pages=550–559|doi=10.1002/j.1537-2197.1967.tb10676.x|bibcode=1967AmJB...54..550H }}</ref> The plants can tolerant some shade as well as drought but need regular watering during the first growing season to build strong roots.

Plants can be grown from [[corm]]s (similar to bulbs and tubers) or from seed, or the plants can be bought at garden centres or nurseries.

To grow from seed, start in early spring either indoors or outside. Germination takes 20–45 days. When leaves appear, divide in large clumps. Plants should be spaced 12-15 inches apart. Spacing allows sun and air to help with potential diseases such as stem rot (''[[Sclerotinia sclerotiorum]]''), leaf spots (''Phyllosticta liatridis,'' ''Septoria liatridis''), rusts (''Coleosporium laciniariae,'' ''Puccinia liatridis''), powdery mildew (''[[Golovinomyces ambrosiae]]'' complex), and wilt (''[[Verticillium albo-atrum]]''). When growing from seed, blooms do not usually appear until the second year.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://wimastergardener.org/article/liatris/|title=Master Gardener Program|website=University of Wisconsin-Extension|access-date=2016-12-14|archive-date=2016-12-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220164848/http://wimastergardener.org/article/liatris/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

If amending the soil, the plants prefer soil with high levels of calcium and magnesium and low levels of potassium and phosphorus.<ref name="Hadley & Levin-1967" />

In gardens, ''Liatris spicata'' works well planted individually, as a border, and because of its vertical form, it contrasts well with mounded and broad-leaf plants. In informal gardens, large sweeps of plantings work well.<ref name="Wisconsin Horticulture" />

The flowers either fresh or dried work well as cut flowers<ref name="Plant Finder"/><ref name="Wisconsin Horticulture" /> and have a [[vanillin|vanilla scent]] when dried.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Sanford|first=J. A.|date=1879|title=Notes from Toledo, Ohio|jstor=2995070|journal=Botanical Gazette|volume= 4| issue = 10|pages=219|doi=10.1086/325289|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Role in ecosystems==
''Liatris spicata'' is excellent for attracting pollinators and beneficial insects. These include butterflies such as the monarch, tiger swallowtail, clouded sulphur, orange sulphur, gray hairstreak, Aphrodite fritillary, painted lady, red admiral, and wood nymphs. The flowers attract bumblebees, digger bees ([[Anthophorini]]), long-horned bees (''Melissodes'' spp.), leaf-cutting bees (''[[Megachile]]'' spp.), skippers, and birds including hummingbirds.<ref name="Wisconsin Horticulture" /><ref name="NPIN" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/nypmctn11164.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150912112805/http://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/nypmctn11164.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 12, 2015|title=Pollinator-Friendly Plants for the Northeast United States|publisher=USDA Natural Resource Conservation Service}}</ref> Caterpillars of the rare glorious flower moth (''Schinia gloriosa'') and liatris flower moth (''[[Schinia sanguinea]]'') feed on the flowers and seeds.<ref name="abnativeplants">{{Cite web|url=http://www.abnativeplants.com/plant/Liatris-spicata|title=''Liatris spicata'' Dense Blazing Star from American Beauties|website=www.abnativeplants.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220163332/http://www.abnativeplants.com/plant/Liatris-spicata|archive-date=2016-12-20|access-date=2025-07-14
}}</ref> Caterpillars of the liatris borer moth (''[[Carmenta anthracipennis]]'') bore through the plant's stems. Groundhogs, rabbits, and voles will also eat the plants.<ref>{{Illinois Wildflowers|wetland/plants/msh_blazingstar|Marsh Blazingstar (Liatris spicata) |access-date=2016-12-07}}</ref>

Deer are less likely to eat ''Liatris spicata'' than other plants and is therefore considered deer-resistant, although deer will eat almost anything when food is scarce.<ref name="abnativeplants" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.easywildflowers.com/quality/deer_resistant_native_plants.htm|title=Deer Resistant Native Plants Wildflowers and Shrubs|website=www.easywildflowers.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190709011812/http://www.easywildflowers.com/quality/deer_resistant_native_plants.htm|archive-date=2019-07-09|access-date=2025-07-14
}}</ref>

==Medicinal uses==
''Liatris spicata'' was historically used medicinally by Native Americans as a [[carminative]], [[diuretic]], [[stimulant]] and [[expectorant]] herb.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://phytochem.nal.usda.gov/phytochem/search|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160415161552/https://phytochem.nal.usda.gov/phytochem/search|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 15, 2016|title=U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service. Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases|date=1992–2016}}</ref><ref name="Hamel & Chiltoskey-1975">{{Cite book|title=Cherokee Plants and Their Uses -- A 400 Year History|last=Hamel, Paul B. and Mary U. Chiltoskey|publisher=Herald Publishing Co.|year=1975|location=Sylva, N.C.|pages=27}}</ref><ref name="Densmore-1932">{{Cite news|url=https://archive.org/details/menomineemusic0000dens|url-access=registration|title=Menominee Music|last=Densmore|first=Francis|date=1932|work=SI-BAE Bulletin|edition=#102|page=[https://archive.org/details/menomineemusic0000dens/page/129 129]}}</ref> In addition to these uses, the [[Cherokee]] used the plant as an [[analgesic]] for pain in the back and limbs and the [[Menominee]] used it for  heart issues. The root/corm of the plant is the part most often used.<ref name="Hamel & Chiltoskey-1975" /><ref name="Densmore-1932" /> Native Americans also used the plant to treat swelling, abdominal pain and spasms/colic, and snake bites.<ref name="Wisconsin Horticulture" /><ref name="Gleason1963" /> Currently, the plant is used for a sore throat by gargling an infusion, as an herbal insect repellent, and in potpourri.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.blm.gov/style/medialib/blm/co/field_offices/ahc/documents.Par.75520.File.dat/Plant_Guide_2013.pdf|title=Bureau of Land Management Anasazi Heritage Center Plant Guide|location=Dolores, CO|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170210054232/https://www.blm.gov/style/medialib/blm/co/field_offices/ahc/documents.Par.75520.File.dat/Plant_Guide_2013.pdf |archive-date=2017-02-10}}</ref>
